blocks.x: I'll make a note we're interviewing Mr. Wilbert Tillman at 1272, this is Johnson, and the date is August 15th, 1961. Would you give your full name, Mr. Tillman? Wilbert Tillman. How's that first name spelled? Is there a T on the end?
W-I-L-B-E-R-T.
Any middle name or initial? No one middle name. Do you mind telling us just when you were born and what part of the town if you came from this city, from New Orleans?
I was born in 1898, 31st day of March.
First day of March?
31st. 31st.
Uh-huh.
I was born right here in Yard.
What part of town did you?
719 Adams Street.

Adams, way uptown. Almost Carlton, is that? That's Carlton, yes. I wonder if you could tell us anything about your family, if your father, mother, any uncles, anybody played music in your family when you were a child? Do you remember any music in your home?
No. No. I had a cousin that played banjo.
What was his name? Joe Baptiste. Oh, Joe Baptiste. I think I've heard him. I know I've heard some of the Baptiste's names before. Uh-huh. Was he older than you, I guess?
Oh, yeah. He's older than me. Did he play with any bands? Do you remember? Yeah, he was playing with different bands, but by me being so small, I mean I wouldn't know the names of the bands. Yeah.
And your father didn't play any instrument? No.
No, my father didn't. In fact, nobody in my family but him at that time. Yeah.

And you were a boy, you remember, up in Carlton, was it all connected right to the city, or was it seemed like another little town up the river? No, it was all connected. All connected to those days. I know at one time they even ran a little railroad up there, you know, a separate town. Yeah.
Well, I was born during the time of the mule cars, but I mean it still was horse cars, they called them at that time.
Run by the city, yeah.
Yeah, that was by the city.
Yeah. Can you tell us about when you first took up music, what your first instrument was, and your teacher, or anyone that you helped you?

Well, I'll tell you. Helped you? When I first started to try to play, I used to play a flute. You know those ten flutes? Oh, yeah. When I was so good on them, everybody tried to encourage me to play music. At that time things were so hard, I mean I never could buy an instrument, you see? But I really could play one of them things. How long were you then? When I was going to school, I must have been around about nine, ten years old.
Was that one of those straight flutes?

The straight ten flutes, yeah, the six hole. And a white fella by the name of Prechter, he happened to find an old cornet laying around his house. After he used to hear me playing that flute all the time, he gave me the cornet. I fooled around with that and played on it and tried to learn a couple of pieces, but I never would call myself a cornet player, you know? I was a little girl. We made up a little band, guitar, I mean at that time they used to be banjos. I was playing the cornet and we had a fella named Lawrence Boynes who was playing clarinet. Lil' Well, he was playing drum. We played around, people used to hire us for little parties. We'd do about five or six pieces, you know? You were all youngsters? All kids, yeah, all kids. So, that went on for a while and around 1917, I decided to join the Navy. Well, I had been gone a little better than a year. And I happened to meet one of John's brothers, which we for his cousins, you know? John Casimir.
Oh, yeah.

I happened to meet one of his brothers over in Bordeaux, France. Well, he had one of John's old clarinets and just had it laying up there. And I told him, I said, well, you got that horn, why don't you give it to me? You ain't using it. For sure enough, he did. And I took John's clarinet and kept it on the boat, fooling around with it, you know, in my spare time. And I came out the Navy 1921, 1920. And I played around here a while. And then finally I decided I'd take lessons and try to learn it right, you know? So, I went to old man John, I'm afraid of taking lessons from him. And I found I was making some slow improvement with him. And I left him and went to Dave Poikins.
That was on the clarinet, did you say?

On the clarinet, yeah. And after I left Dave Poikins, I went to Pinchback T-Roll. I was taking a couple of lessons from the old man Shalini. I was taking a couple of lessons from Edmund Hall. I was taking a couple of lessons from T-Roll. Tio, you remember Tio? Yeah, I didn't know him.
I've heard all about him.
Yeah, I was taking a couple of lessons from him.
That was the younger Lorenzo Tio.

Lorenzo, yeah. Well, by that time I had got to playing pretty good. Then I went and played with, we made up another band, Pellis Band. That was the first real band we made up, you know? And we played Rania and made pretty good hits.
Who was with you in the Pellis Band?

Pellis Band, well at that time we had Nyash Ross on bass. And Alan Gordett on trumpet. I was on clarinet. I can't remember who was playing guitar and drums. But I know that was our first little band, you know? About how many pieces were it? We had six. Six pieces. Six pieces, yeah. Then I, after people found out I could play well, then we started splitting up and getting with different bands. I played with Willie Cornish. I had me and Willie Cornish on trombone. And Octave Crosby on drums. And Sam Toole's on banjo. Oh dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear He had a son named Nat Toad. Oh sure, yeah. He's called W-L-E-S. Yeah, his son's a bass player. Sure, yeah. There was a whole family of musicians. I never did know any of them.
I've seen the name and the picture of their band.

Yeah, well I played with them and then Sam and Cornish got in a little misunderstanding and he split up. And Cornish made up his own band, well I went with Cornish. And I left off a clarinet then and went on sax, and John went in the band on clarinet. Cornish was on trombone and we had Wood and Joe playing Cornish. That was the lineup, you know, in that band. And I played with him a while. And finally Jack Kerris band made a split. And at that time his name was Fame around here, you know. Yeah, her mother, Punchy told us about him. Yeah, well his band split up and I think that was when Punchy first decided to go off. Went off of the show or something like that. Well anyway Jack Kerris taught me and my brother-in-law to join the band. We was young kids and we just wanted to have that name or saying we played with Jack Kerris, you know. So we joined the band and made out pretty good with the exception that he used to cheat us out of our money when we were knocked off. We'd play the jobs and they'd pay us short, you know. Tell us to go around and tell everybody we was playing with Jack Kerris. Well we thought that was a big honor. And we played with Jack for I guess about a year going on just letting him play us and take our money, just glad to be with the band. Him and Willigan. Willigan was his drum player at that time. You heard of Willigan, eh? Jim Willigan? Yeah. What was his name?
I never knew.

He never knew. Well he's one of the old drummers around here. He died long years ago. Well we played on with Jack until finally we started learning a little more about the music again and started getting off again, you know. At that time, I mean the older musicians was always trying to take advantage of the young musicians. They never wanted to treat them fat, you see. So then I got a chance then to switch and play with different bands. I played with Buddy Petit and I played with Chris Kelly for a while. And we decided to make a brass band.
Was that on clarinet or sax or what?
No, I was still on sax and clarinet then I was doubling. With Buddy Petit and Chris? Buddy Petit and Chris. Yeah, and Chris.
When did you take up to sax?

Well I'd taken up to sax, oh, it must have been around about 1924. When the sax first came out, I was about the fifth man in the Orleans that had a sax, a colored man. Yeah, they had just came out and the fellas was behind me about buying one. Well I liked them and everything but I never figured I could play them because I got so used to the clarinet, you know.
Well did you get an alto or a C melody or what kind of? I had an alto.
I bought a B flat soprano first but I didn't like the tone of it. I bought it because it was straight like a clarinet, you know. And I didn't like the tone and I wound up getting an alto.
Where did you get your sax?
The War Lions.
The War Lions.
Yeah. I bought that War Lions and I was playing with Willie Coney's band at the time. I was playing clarinet down there.
Excuse me, who were some of the other early saxes before you?

Who else played sax in those days? The only one that I knew at that particular time was Sidney Carrere. You heard of Sidney Carrere? Yeah. He was the only one that. He was a big heavy fellow. Was he pretty big?
No, Sidney's a little bitty man.
I'm thinking somebody else. Yeah, he's a little bitty fellow.
He played.
Somebody else with a big round face like a- One of his brothers I think is supposed to be Professor.
Professor Carrere.

Oh, that's it. Yeah, they lived out around, around Constance and Dallas somewhere. Raymond Burke once told the clarinetist, you know the white clarinetist, he said he took a lesson or two. From Professor Carrere. Yeah. Yeah.

Well he had a- He made him play on his, blow on his mouthpiece and Raymond got discouraged and quit or something after the first lesson. Just wanted to blow on the mouthpiece without any sax at first, you know. Yeah. He had an embouchure. Well he was a good reed man, Sidney was. But anyway, he was the first man that I saw with a clarinet outside. They had a couple of white boys hands. Yeah. Yeah. He had a little boy. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah, on the front of town side of the bank. They had a place built like an attic, you know, right up over the front of the store. They used to use a six piece band up there every side of that. That was to draw the people into the store. What did they sell? Sell clothes.
Clothing stores.
Yeah, it's a furniture store.
Are they still there?
No, it's a furniture store there now, I see on that corner. It's on the downtown corner of Porterson Rapport. Downtown, Front of Town corner.
Downtown towards the river?
Yeah. Yeah, I think it's got a furniture store there now.
Isn't there a Silverstein's clothing store still in the city somewhere?
No, I don't think so. They got Rubenstein. Oh, maybe it has one. Yeah.
That place is painted sort of a bluish green color, isn't it? No, it is.

Yeah, they sell some kind of furniture or something. Yeah. Well, man, we played on that corner, I guess, for about five, almost ten years. We used to go to Everside Night and on the object side, on the uptown, uptown, back of town corner, used to have a band used to play there. Had a wine store there, Phoenix wine store. Remember the Phoenix? Yeah, I know that part. Phoenix wine store. That's why you used to take the tin can and go in there and get your can of wine for a nickel, draw it yourself out the bar. I've heard of that. Well, Frank Crump and his daddy had a band on that corner. We were just the opposite one another. There's advertising on Portles and Raport. We'd advertise Silverstone, they'd advertise for Phoenix. What time did you start that? We used to start it around about 630 at night and play a quarter to 10, 10 o'clock, 10 o'clock the ladies. Yeah, pretty good.
I never heard anything like that myself lately.

Oh yeah, well, that was the good old days. A whole lot of the good old days things you know I have now. And I played on the bandwagon. You heard about the bandwagon? Well, I played on the bandwagon with Buck Johnson. Had me, Buck Johnson, George Lewis, Abby Williams, and Baby Dot. Baby Dot played auditorium that night and we played the advertising with Buck that day.
Oh yes, I think I heard about it back in the 1940s.

Yeah, well, I played that with Buck. And they had the, at that time, they had the Tulane Brass Band. Well, Tulane, I used to work with them on sax, and John was playing with them on clarinet. That was drummed by Al Landry, Tulane Band. Well, John said if we could make a name for the Tulane Band, why not let's go and pull off and make up a band of ours own. And that's why we organized at the Young Tuxedo, because we pulled out from the Tulane, you see, and John made up his own band.
What year were you playing with the Tulane Band, Wilbur?
The Tulane Band, well, that was...
That after you left Jack Caring?

Oh yeah, Jack was dead then. Yeah, that was in the late years. That was around in the thirties. Around in the thirties, yeah. And, um... After, after we... made up our own little band, well, we wasn't getting much work because we wasn't known at that time, but I still was working with other bands. Now, my first brass band that I would say that I was really a member, you see, because I had started learning trumpet then, but I was taking lessons on the Lewis Demand, I was trying to get away from the reed. I wanted to get on the trumpet then, because there was more demand for the trumpet at that time than there was for the reed. So I started taking lessons from the Lewis Demand, and I still was playing my clarinet, practicing the treble, when I got good enough to play on the trumpet, then I started getting worked with different various bands, you see. And, uh... I played trumpet with the Eureka Band, I played saxophone with the Eureka Band, and the Eureka Band was the one that encouraged me to start playing bass. See, their bass player got sick, and it was just alterating me from one instrument to another. So, after their bass player got sick, they tried to talk to me about getting on the bass. I said, oh man, I don't know nothing about no bass. They said, well, you play trumpet, it's the same thing. I said, oh no, there's a big difference in bass and trumpet. Well, anyway, they had a funeral, leaving from the Two Hand Club. And they went up town and talked to Pete Blanche about allowing me to bass. So, they kept on saying, go get the bass. You make out all right. Well, I went on up there, but the fact of it, I didn't even know how to tune the bass up, you know what I mean? Because I never was interested in the bass, so... I come on out there with the bass that day and tickle me. I could blow it all right, and I just fingered, I got fingered a corner at you, you know? So, when I knocked off that evening, I said, oh man, you sound almost as good as old man too. Because the old man got pretty old, you know? I was more powerful than anything. I said, oh, good. You know, I don't know nothing about no bass, don't kid yourself. I said, yeah, you did good. Well, then I got interested and started trying to learn the bass. I took one lesson on the bass from old man Shala, not Shala Nene. This old bass player man, he died not long ago.
Delmore.

Professor Delmore, yeah. I take one lesson from him. I only wanted to learn the fundamental part of it, because I know the music myself. That is, I wanted to learn the fingering and the different and the treble clef and the bass clef. Because I figured on my new music and I could do it on and learn it myself. I didn't need to take no lesson on it. I had been taking enough lessons on the clarinet and the trumpet. I took lessons on clarinet and trumpet, I never did take that on the sax, I never did take but the one on the bass. I just self-learned instruments. I learned that myself. So then I played with the Eureka band, I played with old man Allie's band. And that was brass band.
Now, I played and- Excuse me, did you ever play string bass at any time in your life? No, I just waited until I got old as I am now to start taking it up.

Yeah, I have old one there and now I've got to try to get somebody to fix it up for me. If I can get it fixed up I believe I could play it. That's the interest I'm really interested in that now, in the string bass. But I've got old one and I want to try to fix it enough for me to play on it before I go buy a good one. I don't want to get no money to buy a good one. You know it might not get played but I have a old one. And for different orchestras I think I've played with practically all of them they have around you and yours.
I was going to ask you, when about was it that you picked up the bass horn in the Eureka band, the peak branch of the bass horn?
Oh that was around 19... About 1945 or 46 somewhere along there.

We were talking about the dance bands, you say you played with Jack Carey, I suppose it would be around the middle 20's you were talking about with Jack Carey. Where did you go from there after you left Jack?

Well after I left Jack, me and my brother in law made up a band called it. We had me on sax and clarinet and my brother in law on trumpet. And we had Joe Avery on trombone. And Sammy Penns on drums. We used my cousin a couple of times on banjo. We had Sammy Penns on banjo. Baptiste? Yeah we used Baptiste on banjo.
What was your brother in law's name the trumpet player again?
Alan Gaudette.
Gaudette.
Gaudette. Yeah he was one of the good ones right now.
Yeah I never was.

Yeah he just died about four or five years ago. He died up in Michigan. Yeah I never endured him. Yeah he taught him many fellas around you know what I mean. Like Anderson and all them boys they all come up onto him you know. They tried to dap his eye there but he was one of the greats right now.
And how long did you play with that band? Joe Everett.

Joe Everett. Joe Everett. Oh we held that band together around about. Well I guess I might as well say up until when Joe died. Cause we broke up his band and then I made up a band and taken him in the band with me and we named it the Tillman and Everett band. But we was playing you know up until his death. He still had that band but we both was working with different bands right on. Cause I mean in this music field if you don't work with different bands you'll never make it. It's not enough night life here for one band to you know just stay together and play together all the time.
Your band was Joe Angry was up at the buzzards club there on the enunciation or someplace?

Joe Well yeah we played for the buzzards so a lot for about it. The first club we played yeah we played for the buzzards we played for the Eleanor's. We played for the Lions and we used to play up in Audubon Park at Tyler's. You ever heard of Tyler's? Joe Oh yeah. Joe Well that's the first place I met Dick Allen. I was playing at Tyler's. Joe And I encouraged Dick to come here he was in the service thing you know. He had us to make a little cut for him. We had.
I remember he made a tape of that.

Joe Yeah. Joe Well they had dude Foster Lewis was playing trumpet on that at that time. And we cut that tape for Dick. Well he left the enemy on the way to California somewhere and I think his friend died. Joe Well when he got out the service he decided to come down here he wanted to see a carnival. He had never seen a carnival. Joe So I told him I said well Dick I think if you come down there you'll like it. Joe Well sure enough he can and he like it enough to make it at home. Joe He stayed down there. Joe That's why whenever he be making them talks he said well Tillman is part of the cause I'm here in Yorlin. Joe He encouraged me to come down here. Joe Which I'm glad to see him down here. Joe You know what I mean he did a whole lot of good things for me. Joe Since he been around here being a stranger in this town you know. Joe So all those kind of things have to be considered you know.
Joe I'm trying to think of those Saturday night dances. Joe I went to only two or three of them I guess. Joe Ten years ago. Joe Was that at the Buzzards Club every other Saturday wasn't it?

Joe Yeah well the Buzzards had one every other Saturday. Joe In fact the Buzzards used to run every other Saturday when we was playing at Tyler's. Joe You see now we used to get that same crowd the same Buzzard crowd used to follow our band up to Tyler's. Joe Yeah. Joe You see. Joe But the Buzzards they had been running every other Saturday night for at least like you say 10 or 12 years. Joe But it was in the old hall. Joe See now after they built the new home well then they started giving them every Saturday night and they just was using colored bands occasionally. Joe You see they was using white bands well. Joe Last time I went by it sounded like a hillbilly band in there.
Joe Yeah.

Joe Yeah. Joe And then they would use colored bands because a couple of them old timers in that club they liked the Joe. Joe And they used to hire Joe. Joe You know Joe's band and Harold Kristoff he carried a band out there once or twice but the colored bands didn't get very much weight in the new hall with the exception of the carnival marches. Joe Yeah. Joe See now they used to hire every carnival. Joe Now when I was playing with the Eureka band we used to play for the Eleanor's. Joe I played for the Eleanor's with the Eureka band for about I guess for about five or six years. Joe Then at that time Garnier had the buzzers. You hear what I'm talking about? Joe Yeah. Joe Yeah. Joe Well he had the buzzers. Knox and all that bunch they was playing with Garnier. Joe Well then after Garnier gave it up then John took it over and I left the Eureka and went with John. And John held it for about five years. And then the Lions there was behind us every year. They wanted to get us. So finally John left the buzzers and went to the Lions. And he could still be playing for the Lions because last year up until last year the Lions hired him but he told them that he's kind of hard of hearing and he had a heart attack. Joe He was sick last year I remember. Joe Yeah he couldn't play so he turned it over to Anderson. Well Anderson tried to get me to play but I told him the hours had got a little bit too much for me. See they come out seven o'clock in the morning and they parade till five in the evening and I had the ulcerized as a leg. Now I can't do all that work. So I told him no I'd rather not bother with it. So the place he called me up and taught me to play with the Zulus with him. He told me it was a short hour. It was a short hour. Joe Yeah it was really good. I was glad I'd take it because they left the river. I went to the river front for nine o'clock and about quarter to twelve it was all over. That was the best one I had ever played. I figured it would go longer than that you see because their hours was usually from nine to five. But last year with all that segregation mess coming up and people scared to come out and tell them don't come on the street what was going to happen and all of them. They kind of had some bearings on the...
Joe Yeah they decided to cut it short. Well they didn't stop a lot of the other places did they?

Joe It didn't go to Gertrude Dennis. Joe No it didn't look like a carnival you know what I mean? You didn't see nothing. There was just very few people in the street and it was nothing exciting. Joe And I played with Buddy Petit up on the dance line. Cronlott and Canel in the old dance line used to be up there.
That was a Jitney dance?
Joe Yeah that was a Jitney.
Yeah.

Well I played with Buddy there. I had been playing in the band. We had been getting a whole lot of work over the lake around Madisonville and Maddenville all over there. He came from over there around Maddenville. Somewhere over there. And he was well known. People liked him you know. And I was playing with the band. Well at that time he had kind of lost his health. He got so sick and weak I would say that I was mostly holding him up letting him you know try to make a piece of bread because I was playing sax. And he had got so weak he couldn't hardly hit off sometimes. He used to make me hit the band off for him. We played up there a while and things like start to go in bed around there and the guy played us a week and ran off with the money and didn't pay off. Well then Buddy got out and so sick then he couldn't play no more and recently after that he died.
What was he sick of? Was there any particular sickness that he had?

Well I wouldn't know exactly but Buddy had so much exposure I mad about running the TV. That's what it looked more like because I never did hear what he died with but that's what he looked more like. He used to drink hard and plenty night exposure, play them dances and go out in the air and all like that. That's where the most of the old musicians died from exposure to help kill itself you know. He get in them hot places and come out with no coats on. A man can track a whole lot of coal like that. It'd feel good to him right then but up in the ages you begin feeling it. And I think that was mostly his trouble. I played with old man Gus Metcalf, Noel Foster. We used to have practice all our work over the lake too around Beter Spring. All the white places, most of the big white places that was giving dances, outings. We used to play over there. I played with Kid Thomas band. I made more money with his band than the band I ever made it with. Yeah?
Was that during the last war or about when was the memory of that?

Yeah, well that was during the last war. Me and Mealy Bones was playing with him. Mealy was playing clarinet and I was playing sax. And Thomas had nice work. In fact he had more work than he could really do. Because we was going down by every Saturday around wrestling, playing for old man LeBlanc. That was a nickel dance too. The nickel dance was popular, you know what I mean, at that time. Especially all throughout the country. We only had a couple of them here in the city. But everywhere you went out of town to play for Whitey was nickel dance.
Where was that on Grand Isle? The theater?

Oh no, that's Raceland. Oh, Raceland over there. Yeah. Of course I went down to Grand Isle. I went down to Grand Isle and played for Tony in Marula. In fact, I was the first, one of the first colored bands went down and played for Tony when he went down there. Because we used to play for him up in Seussbury. He used to have a place up in Seussbury. And he decided to go down to buy, which I don't blame him because there wasn't nothing but money down there. He's a big gambler and he had the dance hall going and gambling and selling seafood and all like that. Well, he really was making his money. But Big Ike Roberson had a band. Me, Ike Roberson, George Lewis, the Albert Fernandez. We were playing with Big Ike Roberson for Tony in Seussbury. And quite naturally when he went down to buy, well, he still took us down there with him. And after I gave the band up, we still went down there. We used to use Frank Crump. Frank Crump on clarinet and sax and I'd play sax and Albert Fernandez on trumpet. And George Guido on banjo. We had a good lineup down there. We had been playing with dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
I usually get up around that time anyway.
I was going to ask some more. You were talking about these bands like working with Kid Thomas. You might as well go on from there. Is there anything else you want to continue along that line?

Well, yeah, like I said, I played with Thomas. I made more money with him than any band I played with. How kind of money did you make? Did Kips, you mean? Well, in average it was more money but less money. You see, the skills wasn't like it is now. We wasn't in the union. And we was making around $8 and $10 going out of town. That's why we was getting more out of town work, you see. And we played the jobs around there in town. Some of them wasn't paying but a dollar and a dollar and a quarter a night. Two dollars. Two and a half and you made two dollars right there, you was making big money. So that's why we used to grab for all the out of town works. And Thomas had built up a nice reputation.
Was that in the Depression or during the war or before the war? Well, that was... When you were paying a dollar and a dollar and a half an hour, it must have been Depression, but it did.

Not an hour. Man, I played all night. I played all night at the Popeye for a dollar. Oh, really? People be going to work down there at 8 o'clock at night and people be going to work. 6 o'clock in the morning. We'd be playing. Balls stand on the back and say, there'll come a whole lot of people. People be going to work, wouldn't be starting about the night light. And he'd think that there's coming into the place. Come on, hear the tune, hear the tune. We'd talk to battle and oh, man. I played with Octave Crosby out there on Drys Street. They had a dance hall out there on Drys between Melphamine and Texaco. We played there, oh God knows how many years, a dollar and a quarter night, but a dollar and a quarter and a kiddie. Your kiddie would run sometime $5 and $6 a man. That's where you'd make it up. But at the actual price, what we were playing, it was sad. I was glad when the union come about so we could get in the union and get, you know, a fair price. Of course, the union scale was down a long time too before they came up to the mark that there is now. The union scale, when they first started there, was a dollar an hour. Well, you'd play four hours, you still wouldn't make the $4. So it was a long time before the bracket got up where we could get anything. Now, funerals, we used to play funerals, we'd get two and a half to three dollars was topped. We played carnival parade from six o'clock. I played carnival parade for Eleanor Club from six o'clock in the morning to six o'clock in the evening. Didn't make for $10. See, them was the bad times, but the good times, like I say, it was less money but more money. Why I said more money? Because we had more work. You was working more regularly. You know, we had more places. All the little bill gardens and things had four and five piece bands on them. And a couple of those white places was running every night. Well, that told musicians, you know, to have a little something to do. Now, me and Dude and Octave and Drum Player worked out there on Drive Street for a number of years. We used to make a dollar and a quarter of a night, but we made nice tips. Then I played with Dude's Brothers Band, Foster Lewis. He had a band and we used to travel around on percentage. Going all out through Mississippi, Moss Point, Pickyune, Laurel, Lumberton, Hazelwood, Crystal Springs, Hatterboy. He was covering that territory, Burgaloo, but go all played, but it was on percentage. Sometimes what we'd make good on this job and make three or four jobs would be so bad, it would eat up all the expense. Make a trip sometime, I'd go away and stay away a week or two weeks. Come back home maybe with a dollar, a dollar and a half, sometimes nothing. So I decided I would just give up that kind of travel and I said it don't make sense just going around playing to be playing and then getting nothing out of it. Which at that time, things, everybody mostly, you know, smaller bands was traveling around the road on percentage like that, trying to see what they could pick up. And I used to go over the lake with Gus Metcalfe every fall and play those fairs, play the Franklinton Fair and the Covington Fair. Well, that would be a nice pick up. They'd pay you $10 a day and blow it a large on that. Well, that used to, you know, mean something to us. Trying to think of some other band I worked around with.
I asked you about the Lewis, the Lewis's, you said there were brothers, there was Foster Lewis and there was Dude Lewis?

Yeah. What was the Dude's name? Well, I'll tell you the truth, I know that wasn't the right name but it was the only name known by the musicians. They called one of them Dude, Dude was the trumpet player and Forstown was the trombone player.
What was his name?
Forstown.
Forstown.
Forstown. Forstown.
Forstown Lewis. Oh, I thought it was Foster.

Well, that's what I'm saying. You see, that's forstown is Creole. Oh, I see. I see. Yeah. Forstown Lewis is the right name. But now, I don't know if Dude had another name but that was his only known name to the musicians. Dude, you see, because all the musicians called him.
You say Dude was the trumpet player?

Dude was the trumpet player and Forstown was the trombone player. Trombone player. And a good one too. He couldn't read but boy, he had a tone and a trombone. Yes, sir. Yeah, that was two brothers was good for say country boys and just liked his self. I mean, if Dude was living now, he would be right in the demands of the style of trumpet playing that they want to be. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He played just on that style and type, you know?
You say they were from the country somewhere.
Yeah, they came from, I don't know exactly, I don't know if they, what they were born in the class, I know it's in the country. Yeah, they came from the country boys.
Yeah, they came from the country boys.
And they didn't learn music here, they liked music in the country, they come here playing. Of course they had been around here for a number of years but originally their home is in the country.

I was going to ask some more about, to go way back to your childhood again. This little tin flute you played, where did you play that? Did you learn that just watching anybody or learning the street or where did you play it?

I just picked it up myself. I mean, at that time the kids was, they was buying them but just blowing them, you know? Yeah. But I went on and got me one and I used to play songs on it. I could play it real good. And people used to like to, you have me play it like on Saturday evening, man, I'd get on the grocery car and blow that thing and I didn't know what kiddie was but people would get a big kick out of it, you know? Like a bunch of white people might pass in the court and see me blowing and stopping. First thing you know, they draw big congregation around. Every crowd of the Yemi play the flute. Yeah, I often talk about that. I say, some instruments are mad and it's gifted to a poet. I mean, I could take one of them things and play any song on it that I would get.
Somebody told me once some of the kids used to play them on the parades, like the second line kids. I never did see any of that. Did they ever do that?

Oh, no. Yeah, well we all used to play behind the second line. You see, the second line wasn't like the yesterday. I mean, it's run away with it now. You can't get to see a club for a second line. In the olden times it was different. You see now they would have the tally holes. You remember the tally holes? Well, they used to have the tally holes. And most likely the women would be in the tally holes. They'd have the tally holes all decorated with paper ribbon and things. And the men would walk in front and the tally holes behind. The second liners would stay on the bank and they didn't just have to have five or six policemen to try to keep it. You could get a viewing of the parade, what it looked like, you know. And we kids would be on the bank with them floots, like you said, blowing them. But we couldn't go like the kids go now. We maybe could go three or four blocks and we'd turn around and go back home. But our parents didn't allow us further than that, you know. What did you do?
Try to play the same piece right along with the band?

Yeah, you'd be trying to play what they would be playing. And we'd go three or four blocks and then get in another section and pick up maybe a gang of floots. Or maybe a gang of flute players or tin pan players there. They'd beat on boxes and things. Go ahead and have their portion on the sidewalk. You know, file in the parade and they'd go their distance and they had to come back. Because there was more restriction on the kids then than there is now. You see, that old fire in John House up there on Maple Street. And that bell used to ring every night at nine o'clock. Sometime I'd be four and five blocks off from my house when it first hit. But by the time it finished it, I'd be home and sometimes I'd be so scared I'd jump in the bed with my feet full of mud. Be scared to stop the washing. That's just how strict the older people was then. But now the majority of the people, they don't even know where they children is.
When that bell rang, if you were out on the street, could any adult sort of accost you, tell you to go home? Or what would happen to you?

Well, they wouldn't have to do it. They could do it, but they wouldn't have to do it. Because I mean all the children was under that same fit. They had to be inside for nine o'clock. The bell started to ring at nine. I would say about five minutes to nine. It stopped at nine. But by the time it stopped, them kids were off the street. And when you saw children out after that hour, they'd be out with their parents. Some of their parents would have them.
You'd have to be out with an adult.
Yeah, I mean it wasn't a compolter law. It was a compolter family law. I mean the city didn't compol you to be off. But your people is the one that would put that law on you.
Where was the location of that N. John house?

That was on Maple between Boydette and Foyan. Yeah, that's all residential up there now. Yeah, that old N. John house stayed there for many years. Many of the old times, especially from Caldoun, can tell you about that old N. John house. The old N. John house and the old 9th Precinct. That's two old places they'd never forget. 9th Precinct and the Foyan John.
When did you move downtown? How old were you down this move?

When I moved down, I moved from Caldoun. I was around about, I must have been about 12, 18 years old. My mother moved from, well she moved from 719 Adams Street to 7605 Hanson. My father died on Adams Street. And quite a night until after he died, well his sisters and brothers wanted to part out the property that forced my grandmother to sell, you see. Well then my mother rented a house right around the corner, 7605 Hanson Street. And we stayed there and when we left, we stayed there, well I was the oldest, I was around about, between 11 and 12 anyway. And she moved down, she got a house down Cadiz and Willow. Well that's where all my sisters and brothers and me, we all was raised up there right on Cadiz and Willow. Well, by me being the oldest, my father was dead and trying to help to educate the other kids. That caused me to have to quit school young. You see, when we moved from Caldoun, I had got out of school to go to work to help my mother. Because at that time, women was making a very, very small sire. They was getting around four or five dollars a day, something like that. For children to take care of that kind of sire was pretty hard. Although the people wouldn't pay much, and you know, mothers that had plenty of children, they used to give them all the overs and things like that to bring home at night, you know. Stale bread, anything that was left from today's meal. Well that helped the families to go along, see. So I tell you, I didn't come up with no silver spoon in my mouth. I come up a hard way. My daddy died when I was a kid. And like I said, my mother had three other children to try to school. I used to have to get them off to school in the morning, fix their lunch and thing, and then get out. I used to go around and cut grass for people. Make little changes. Deliver milk in the evening. I had all kinds of little jobs. I was trying to learn to plaster and tread. My paran took me and he was giving me 25 cents a week. He used to give my mother a dollar and a half for my earning, but he'd give me 25 cents for my spending chance. And try to learn me to tread, which it did benefit me in the near future, because I did it enough to, you know, get some money out of it. But I worked on the riverfront. And I've been a Pullman porter. I came back and I worked for the IC Railroad Freight Shed. I run on steam ships after I come out the Navy. I went all down Havana, Cuba, Panama, Cristobal, Bocas, Indonesia. I went to France. Well, different parts of France. I went to Saint-Nazaire, and Bordeaux, and Marseille, and Brest. So I did quite a bit of traveling. And then the Pullman service, well, I've been practically in all the states, in the United States, except in, what do you call that place there where it's supposed to be so cool, Bob ran right there not long ago?
Yeah, you don't mean Canada, do you?
Canada. I went everywhere. You don't have to watch them. Yeah, I went to practically all of them except Canada. I never did get to go to Canada.
Well, I was wondering about parades when you were a boy. Were there many parades up in Carleton you can remember?

Well, no, there wasn't many parades. You see, because at that time they only had one club. That club, just like you see, that's one of the oldest original clubs they got around here. The merry-go-round. The merry-go-round, that's right. And see, I don't know much about this downtown section, what was happening, but that merry-go-round, that was organized way back in years. I was a small kid in Carleton. I remember that club. And it's still going on, and it's still in the same location where it was at that time.
Same place.

Same location where it was. So I considered about one of the oldest pleasure clubs they got around here. I mean, that still didn't exist. Yeah, all the rest of them, they make up and they stay a while and they break up. There ain't never much to it. Now, the merry-go-round, I was too small to know what band, which I believe I do know what band was playing for them too. I think Amos Raleigh had a band at that time that used to do that work for the merry-go-round. I don't know, definitely, but I think he's the band that was playing for them in those days. Now, they used to parade every year. They never changed their parade day, their month. They always parade the full Sunday in August. They never changed it. I mean, it just gone on and on for years in different centuries, but it's still that same full Sunday in August. So, there's so much for that. The colors, I don't think they ever changed their colors because the men wear white pants and blue shirts, and the women wear white dresses and blue blouses. So, that changed, they claimed that's something represented to the sky. I don't know what feature it is to them, but I mean, that's what they- That's some meaning to everybody. Yeah, that's some meaning of it. Now, another thing was popular in them days that died out, that was the advertisements. You see, everywhere they would give a dance like St. Elizabeth or St. Catherine, the economy, the cooperators hall. Where was St. Elizabeth's hall? St. Elizabeth's hall was on Valance between Camp and Cadiz. I mean, on camp between Valance and Cadiz. Yeah, that was St. Elizabeth's hall. It's still there, do you remember now? I don't remember. No, they tore it down. They got houses long there.
And the cooperators, maybe we can get the location of that. That's still there, that's the Hope's hall.
Yeah, that's the Hope's hall.
The church on there. That's right. The Zion, that's right. That's right. And the Zion is saying-
That's right. And the Zion is saying-
